EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – Medicaid Expansions and Children’s Health, 1987-1994

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Primary method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event–study extension.

Why appropriate:
•  Medicaid expansions generated plausibly exogenous variation across states, time, age-groups, and income cut-offs.  
•  NHIS/CPS supply repeated cross-sections that straddle multiple expansion waves (1986, 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991).  
•  DID absorbs all permanent state factors (supply of providers, baseline health, political environment) and all nationwide shocks (macro-cycle, vaccine roll-outs), isolating the policy-driven change.  
•  Event-study coefficients allow visual and statistical pre-trend tests and dynamic treatment-effect profiling.

Extension (second stage / robustness): 2SLS where a “simulated eligibility rate” serves as an instrument for actual Medicaid take-up, following Currie–Gruber (1996) style.  The first stage isolates policy-driven, not behaviour-driven, changes in coverage.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control Definition
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable
  Eligible_ist = 1 if child i of age a in state s and survey year t has family income below the Medicaid income threshold that applied to age group a in state-year (s,t).

Control units
  (i) Children with similar demographics in states-years where they are still ineligible, and  
  (ii) Slightly older children in the same state-year who were not covered by the contemporaneous expansion wave (age-group DID).  
Using both sets mitigates composition bias.

Treatment timing
  Expansion effective date is the month the state implemented the federally authorised option.  For NHIS/CPS (annual), a child is considered treated in calendar year t if the expansion was in force ≥ 6 months of that calendar year.

Continuous treatment (for some checks)
  EligShare_st = share of a 1987 baseline micro-sample of children who would be eligible in (s,t) given the new rules – our simulated eligibility.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends. In the absence of Medicaid rule changes, outcomes for eligible versus ineligible children would have evolved similarly within a state, and across states.  
 Plausibility: Disease environment, technology, and secular trends in paediatric care were nationwide.  State-specific linear trends will further relax the assumption.

A2. No differential contemporaneous shocks. No other state policy systematically coincides with Medicaid expansions and differentially affects only the newly eligible age/ income cells.  
 Plausibility: S-CHIP and large welfare reforms occur after our sample window; still control for state-year AFDC generosity and unemployment.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA). A child’s outcome depends only on her own eligibility, not on others’ eligibility (low spillovers).  Some spillovers through clinic crowding are possible but assumed small.

A4. Exogeneity of migration. Families are not moving across states in response to expansions in a way correlated with potential outcomes.  Supported by short implementation lags and moving costs; will test on CPS mobility items.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Differential pre-trends.  
 • Event-study coefficients on leads; formally test β_{k<0}=0.  
 • Add state-specific linear trends; results robust?

T2. Measurement error in family income → misclassification of eligibility.  
 • Use CPS annual income (more accurate) where possible.  
 • Discretise income into broad bins (e.g., % FPL deciles) so that small errors do not flip treatment status.  
 • IV using simulated eligibility share to attenuate attenuation bias.

T3. Concurrent state health initiatives (e.g., immunisation drives, provider taxes).  
 • Control vector of state-year policies collected from KFF and NASBO.  
 • Sensitivity: drop states with known contemporaneous child-health programs.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
############################################################
# 0.  Packages
############################################################
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dimensional fixed-effects
library(haven)         # if Stata dta files exist
library(lubridate)
library(modelsummary)

############################################################
# 1.  Data loading
############################################################
nhis <- read_csv("NHIS_children_87_94.csv")   # one row per child
cps  <- read_csv("CPS_children_87_94.csv")

rules <- read_csv("Medicaid_rules_ages_income_by_state_year.csv")
# rules: state, year, age_low, age_high, income_threshold_pctFPL

############################################################
# 2.  Variable construction
############################################################
# Harmonise NHIS & CPS into long panel
data <- bind_rows(nhis %>% mutate(survey="NHIS"),
                  cps  %>% mutate(survey="CPS"))

# Define Medicaid eligibility
data <- data %>%
  left_join(rules, by = c("state","year")) %>%
  mutate(eligible = if_else(age >= age_low & age <= age_high &
                            income_pctFPL <= income_threshold_pctFPL, 1, 0))

# Outcomes
data <- data %>%
  mutate(doctor_visits = as.numeric(doctor_visits),
         hospital_nights = as.numeric(hospital_nights),
         good_health = if_else(gen_health %in% c("Excellent","Very good"),1,0))

# Controls
data <- data %>%
  mutate(female = if_else(sex=="Female",1,0),
         black = (race=="Black"),
         hisp  = (hispanic==1))

############################################################
# 3.  Main DID specification
############################################################
did_spec <- feols(doctor_visits ~ eligible + female + age + black + hisp |
                    factor(state) + factor(year), 
                  data = data, cluster = ~state)
etable(did_spec)

############################################################
# 4.  Event study using Sun & Abraham interaction
############################################################
data <- data %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  mutate(first_treat = min(year[eligible==1])) %>%
  ungroup()

es_spec <- feols(doctor_visits ~ sunab(first_treat, year) + 
                   female + age + black + hisp |
                   state + year, data = data, cluster = ~state)
iplot(es_spec)   # pre-trend check

############################################################
# 5.  IV robustness: simulated eligibility -> Medicaid coverage
############################################################
# Create simulated eligibility within each state-year
baseline87 <- data %>% filter(year==1987)
sim_share <- baseline87 %>%
  select(state, age, sex, race, hisp, income_pctFPL) %>%
  crossing(year = 1987:1994) %>%   # create each year’s rule context
  left_join(rules, by=c("state","year")) %>%
  mutate(sim_elig = if_else(income_pctFPL <= income_threshold_pctFPL,1,0)) %>%
  group_by(state,year) %>%
  summarise(sim_elig_share = mean(sim_elig), .groups='drop')

data <- left_join(data, sim_share, by=c("state","year"))

iv_spec <- feols(doctor_visits ~ 1 | medicaid_covered ~ sim_elig_share +
                   female + age + black + hisp | state + year,
                 data = data, cluster = ~state)
etable(iv_spec)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory: Removing financial barriers boosts preventive and curative utilisation.  
Prior magnitude:  
• Outpatient visits ↑ 10–15 % (≈ 0.3–0.5 additional visits per child-year).  
• Hospital nights ↓ 5–8 %.  
• Share in “excellent/very good” health ↑ 2–3 p.p.  
Stronger effects among poorest quartile and for chronic-condition sub-sample.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist (DID) – Self-Assessment
1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable / fails

C1. Well-defined treatment & timing ………………… 1  
C2. Parallel pre-trends documented (event-study) … 1  
C3. No simultaneous confounding policies ………… 0.5  
C4. Stable composition of treated & control ……… 0.5  
C5. Correct inference (state-clustered SEs) ……… 1  

Total: 4/5 – credible but hinges on mitigating concurrent policy shocks and mobility-induced composition changes.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of plan
